workTitle: String Quartet No. 14 in C-sharp minor, Op. 131

clues.label: A musical characteristic
clues.text: Seven movements, no pause between them. And it doesn't open with a fast movement like you'd expect — it opens with a slow fugue.

clues.label: Places the composer lived and worked
clues.text: Born in a Rhineland town, but he spent his whole adult life in one imperial capital further east — and he kept changing apartments. Dozens of times.

clues.label: A historical event connected to the composer
clues.text: 1802. His hearing is getting worse and he is not in a good place. Staying in a village outside the city, he writes a private letter to his brothers. Nobody sees it until after he dies.

clues.label: A biographical detail
clues.text: By the time he wrote this he was basically deaf. Visitors had to write their half of the conversation in notebooks — and those notebooks are still around.

clues.label: An anecdote
clues.text: Two years earlier: first night of his ninth symphony. Last movement is that huge choral tune everyone knows as Ode to Joy. He is completely deaf, standing there beating time to music he cannot hear, and a singer has to spin him around so he can see people cheering.

explanation.summary: The deafness, the seven linked movements, and the path from the Rhine to the imperial capital: Ludwig van Beethoven, writing in Austria in 1826.

points.text: Seven movements glued together, opening with a fugue — that's the C-sharp minor Quartet, Op. 131.
The Rhineland town is Bonn. The capital is Vienna, where he lived from 1792 until he died, and where this quartet was written.
That 1802 letter is the Heiligenstadt Testament, written in what was then a village north of Vienna.
Total deafness in the last decade, plus the conversation books. If you know one biographical fact about him, it's this.
Ninth Symphony, Ode to Joy, deaf, turned to face the applause. Vienna, May 1824. The singer is usually named as Caroline Unger.
